$comment: T-3578 format, the smooth style (T-3696; docs/AUDIO.md § Narration style): the same words as the panel shows, with ElevenLabs v3 audio tags in square brackets and [short pause]/[long pause] and ellipses for pauses, a pause at each change of subject, no whispering, at most one laugh. Performance only: a tone is a reading, not evidence of how anyone spoke (L-jaunt-voices-3578). Keyed <part>:<id>.

scripts.opening:opening:
[measured] Chicago's First Murder.

[short pause] Chicago in 1812 is a small, crowded place: a garrison of about fifty soldiers under Captain Nathan Heald, a government trading house, and a few houses on the north bank. [short pause] Everyone knows everyone, and the two men who will meet at the gate have been rivals for years: over a house, over the soldiers' trade, and over how to treat their neighbours as war with Britain comes closer.

[short pause] Nine stops: the killing first, then from 1804 to the night of the killing and the morning after, with the time of day and the season set for each. [short pause] Three versions are told side by side: the Kinzie family's, told for a century; a girl's who watched from inside the fort; and the letters the factor and the surgeon's mate sent to Washington within weeks.

[short pause] The story starts at the end: outside the gate of Fort Dearborn, at sunset on 17 June 1812.
scripts.stop:cold-open: [gravely] 17 June 1812, sunset, outside the gate of Fort Dearborn. [short pause] Jean Lalime, the fort's interpreter, lies dead in the dust, stabbed. The man walking away, bleeding from the shoulder, is John Kinzie, the trader who sells to the garrison, the man later histories would call 'The Father of Chicago'. [short pause] Who did it has never been in doubt. Why, and whether it was murder, depends on whom you believe. [short pause] To see how it came to this, go back eight years, across the river, to the best house in Chicago.
scripts.stop:du-sable-house: [measured] Eight years earlier. [short pause] May 1804, morning. This is the best house in Chicago, built by Jean Baptiste Point du Sable, the trader who settled here first. [short pause] In 1800 he sold out, and the deed recorded in Detroit names the buyer as Jean Lalime, a French interpreter and trader, with the money from their shared employer, the fur trader William Burnett. [short pause] The witness who signed it was John Kinzie, another of Burnett's traders. Now Kinzie moves his family in and makes it his. No record of any sale from Lalime to Kinzie has been found. [short pause] The family later said Kinzie bought the place from a 'Le Mai', and historians long treated 'Lalime' as a misspelling of that name. Lalime did not leave. [short pause] He moved a few doors west, close enough to watch Kinzie live in his house.
scripts.stop:lalime-house: [measured] Seven years later. [short pause] 26 May 1811, afternoon. Lalime had wintered in the big house in 1803-04 with the fort's first surgeon, who called him 'a very decent man and a good companion'. [short pause] When Kinzie took it, Lalime moved here, to a smaller house west along the bank, and became the fort's interpreter, the man who speaks for the garrison with its neighbours. [short pause] Today he writes to Governor William Clark at St. Louis: 'An Indian from the Peorias passed here yesterday' with word of horses stolen from the southern settlements. His letters show, Kirkland wrote, 'a man of ability and education'. [short pause] Across the river, a new arrangement is about to make Kinzie richer, and Lalime his enemy.
scripts.stop:factory: [measured] Nine months later. [short pause] 10 March 1812, morning, at the factory. This is the government's own trading house, run at cost by the factor, Matthew Irwin. The sutler is different: a private merchant licensed to sell to the soldiers. [short pause] In January Captain Nathan Heald, the fort's commander, made 'Messrs. Kinzie & Forsyth', Kinzie's trading firm, the garrison's only sutlers. Today Irwin writes to Washington that the pair had offered someone '400$ per annum' to win them the post. [short pause] Two men side with Irwin: the young surgeon's mate, Isaac Van Voorhis, and the interpreter, Lalime. Kinzie, an older officer once wrote, was 'a man of ungovernable temper'. [short pause] Within weeks, a quarrel over money becomes talk of killing.
scripts.stop:bad-blood: [measured] Five weeks later. [short pause] 16 April 1812, the officers' barracks. Ten days ago men 'supposed to be Winnebagoes' killed two farmhands at Hardscrabble, up the South Branch. Fear has turned on everyone. [short pause] Irwin writes today that 'Propositions were openly made to murder' neighbours who had always been peaceable, French settlers among them, and names who pushed hardest: 'the Suttler for this garrison & his Son-in law—Lt Helm'. [short pause] That is Kinzie and Lieutenant Linai Helm, the fort's second officer, married to Kinzie's stepdaughter. Ensign George Ronan, the youngest officer, threatens to shoot Lalime. Helm swears to scalp the factor. [short pause] In May, Heald arrests Helm for plotting to kill six Sauk men who had come in peace, then lets him go. By June everyone at the fort has chosen a side. [short pause] On the evening of the 17th they are all on the parade.
scripts.stop:the-quarrel: [measured] Two months later. [short pause] 17 June 1812, about six in the evening, inside the fort. Tomorrow, in Washington, Congress will declare war on Britain; the news will not reach this fort until the middle of July. [short pause] On the parade Helm rails against the factor, and ends, as Van Voorhis wrote, 'by saying he would give a very handsome treat if the Factory would be done away!' Kinzie backs his son-in-law. [short pause] Lalime stands up for Irwin's store: he 'defended the pure motives and just dealings of the Institution'. Voices rise. Then Kinzie and Lalime walk out of the gate together. The gates are about to close for the night. [short pause] Only one of the two men will walk back.
scripts.stop:the-gate: [gravely] An hour later. [short pause] 17 June, sunset, back outside the main gate. Victoire Porthier, a girl inside the fort, remembered: 'It was sunset, when they used to shut the gates of the fort.' [short pause] She heard Helm call out to Kinzie to look out for Lalime, 'as he had a pistol.' 'We heard the pistol go off and saw the smoke. Then they fell down together.' Kinzie got up, bleeding from the shoulder. [short pause] Lalime did not; he had been stabbed. Irwin, the factor, saw it all from twenty or thirty yards. Van Voorhis wrote that 'it was a perfect assassination and can be proven to be such'. The Kinzie family called it self-defence. [short pause] A man is dead at the gate, the killer is the commander's sutler and the lieutenant's father-in-law, and the officers must decide what to do with him.
scripts.stop:the-flight: [measured] Four hours later. [short pause] 17 June, about 11:20 at night. Irwin's account: Ensign Ronan told Kinzie to run, Helm hid him in the garrison about four hours, then walked him down to the river's edge, shook his hand and let him go. [short pause] The family's account: Kinzie 'returned to the house covered with blood', and his wife took him into the woods, where 'she dressed his wounds' and kept him hidden for days. [short pause] Porthier's account: 'In the night he packed up some things and my father took him to Milwaukee'. Three versions of one night. [short pause] At the gate, Lalime's body is still lying where it fell.
scripts.stop:the-grave: [solemnly] Nine hours later. [short pause] 18 June, morning. The townspeople want an inquest, a public inquiry into the death. Irwin wrote that instead 'a file of soldiers headed by Lt. Helm carried it away by force'. [short pause] Lalime was buried on this bank, about 'two hundred yards west of the Kinzie house', inside a picket fence, in plain view of the house he had once owned on paper. [short pause] In 1891 men digging a cellar near Cass and Illinois streets found a skeleton in 'a rude pine coffin', and the bones went to the Chicago Historical Society.
scripts.ending:verdict:
[measured] That night Heald ordered the factor to help arrest Kinzie. [short pause] Irwin refused and was turned out of the garrison; Heald's own letter says why: 'a Citizen who had but a few days previous stabed an other citizen to the heart in your presence'. [short pause] Irwin left on 5 July and was taken prisoner at Mackinac. Van Voorhis died on the lake shore on 15 August. [short pause] Kinzie lived, came back in 1816, and his family told the story for a century.

[short pause] So was it murder? Historians still disagree, and they disagree sharply.

[short pause] THE CASE AGAINST KINZIE. Irwin, writing after the fall of the fort, accused him of worse than murder: of helping bring on the disaster of 15 August, and so 'destroying the Witnesses to the murder of Lalime'. [short pause] Milo Quaife, the historian who found Irwin's letters, warned in 1915 that to readers who saw Kinzie 'as a kind of demigod', that charge 'will come as a distinct shock'. [short pause] The Chicago Reader in 2018 called the self-defence story 'a popular lie': Lalime was 'stabbed to death in broad daylight and cold blood', one of 'three forgotten men who tried and failed to end the corruption, bribery, and smuggling' at the fort. [short pause] 'Kinzie was behind it all, the doctor and factor alleged.'

[short pause] THE CASE FOR KINZIE. In the family's telling, Lalime, 'insanely jealous over Kinzie's success as a trader, treacherously attacked him'. [short pause] Currey (1912) says an officers' inquiry found 'a verdict of justifiable homicide', and Hubbard said 'Mr. Kinzie deeply regretted the killing of Lalime'. Porthier, the girl at the gate: 'You see Kinzie wasn't to blame at all.' [short pause] And then: 'That is what they all said.'

[short pause] WHO TOLD IT. Quaife: only the version 'originating with the relatives and friends of the slayer gained the public ear', and it 'put the onus of the affray on the slain'. [short pause] The Reader: 'The winners didn't write the history books.'

[short pause] Lalime's bones are still in a box in the Chicago History Museum's storage. You have stood where he fell. [short pause] Decide for yourself.
